### 2. Dated Facts Moving This Case Away from the Base Rate
* **Scheduled Election Window (Direction: Confirms event timing):** On November 24, 2026, Taiwan's Central Election Commission (CEC) confirmed that nearly 19.6 million people are eligible to vote in the "nine-in-one" local elections scheduled for Saturday, November 28, 2026. There are no typhoons, emergencies, or legal disruptions threatening the voting schedule.
* **Two-Way Race Structure and KMT–TPP Consolidation (Direction: Toward YES):** Unlike the three-way race in 2022 (where the anti-DPP vote was split between Chiang Wan-an and TPP-backed Huang Shan-shan), the 2026 contest is effectively a head-to-head race between KMT incumbent Chiang Wan-an and DPP nominee Puma Shen (沈伯洋), alongside four minor party/independent candidates polling at or below 1%. On November 21, 2026, former Taipei Mayor and TPP founding chairman Ko Wen-je appeared on stage with Chiang Wan-an at a major rally in Taipei to publicly endorse Chiang's re-election. In the November 16, 2026 TVBS poll, 83% of TPP-identifying voters expressed support for Chiang.
* **Pre-Blackout Polling Shows a Tightened Race (Direction: Away from the high base rate toward 50%):** Under Taiwan's election law, publishing or citing polls is banned during the final 10 days before election day (starting November 18). In the final "blackout polls" (封關民調) released on November 16–17, 2026, the race had narrowed substantially from Chiang's 28-point lead in May. Mainstream institutional polls showed Chiang with a narrow edge or within the margin of error: TVBS (Nov 16) had Chiang at 46% and Shen at 44%; ETtoday (Nov 16) had Chiang at 48.1% and Shen at 42.0%; and Apollo/艾普羅 (Nov 17) had Chiang at 44.1% and Shen at 37.1%. Conversely, Fengcan Media (鋒燦傳媒, Nov 16) showed Shen at 44.7% to Chiang's 43.0%, and two green-leaning think tanks (Shinmin Association and Taiwan Strategy Institute) showed double-digit raw leads for Shen (48.6% to 33.8% and 52.6% to 35.3%), though Shinmin's own turnout-adjusted model projected the actual vote share at 48.3%–52.2% for Chiang versus 48.0%–52.0% for Shen.
* **Turnout Dynamics and Late Rally Controversies (Direction: Mixed / Slight uncertainty):** On November 25, 2026, *CommonWealth Magazine* reported on the "Ocean Current" (洋流) grassroots movement supporting Puma Shen, noting estimates that youth enthusiasm could boost Taipei's turnout by 5 to 7 percentage points, though also mobilizing counter-turnout for the KMT. On November 26, 2026, Focus Taiwan reported that Shen canceled his in-person Friday election-eve rally on Ren'ai Road following commuter backlash over multi-day lane closures and a controversy over Chiang's team booking prime rally venues within 0.35 seconds.

### 3. Strongest Reason the Obvious Outcome Might Fail
While Chiang holds the structural advantages of incumbency, municipal administrative satisfaction, and formal Blue-White (KMT-TPP) consolidation, his lead in standard telephone polls shrank dramatically over the six months leading up to the polling blackout. If Puma Shen's grassroots "Ocean Current" movement generates an unprecedented surge in youth and first-time voter turnout (pushing overall Taipei turnout well above 70%), or if young voters were systematically under-sampled by traditional polling methodologies prior to the November 18 blackout, Shen could narrowly overtake Chiang in the final count.

Balancing Taipei'span-Blue structural advantage, the lack of a third-party spoiler, Ko Wen-je's explicit endorsement of Chiang, and Chiang's leads in TVBS and ETtoday against the genuine tightness of the pre-blackout polling averages, I estimate a 68% probability that Chiang Wan-an wins re-election.

The Taipei mayoralty has a strong long-run pan-blue lean: the DPP has won it only once since the 1990s, and in 2022 Chiang took 42.3 percent in a three-way race while the DPP managed only 31.9 percent. Incumbent re-election is the modal outcome in Taiwan’s special municipalities when the officeholder runs again, which would put a prior near 60 percent before this year’s evidence. That prior is pulled down sharply by the polling collapse. Chiang led by roughly 25–28 points in May; by the final legal window in mid-November the same race was inside or near the margin of error in most surveys, with several non-blue pollsters showing Shen ahead and even blue-leaning ones reduced to a 2-point Chiang edge (TVBS) or a larger but disputed one. TPP identifiers are consolidating heavily behind Chiang (above 90 percent in multiple surveys), which is already visible in the numbers, and older pan-blue turnout reliability plus possible non-response still help the incumbent. No polls have been publishable since the statutory blackout began at midnight on 18 November, so the last ten days of campaigning are unmeasured; KMT sources claimed the “ocean wave” had stalled, but that is unverified. The election itself is on the statute calendar for 28 November and there is no indication it will be moved.
